concepts.label: Gardening
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize gardening as a range of plant-growing settings rather than only an outdoor vegetable plot.
concepts.card: Gardening means growing plants for food, flowers, or decoration in a chosen space. That space can be a plot, balcony, or container. Comparing these settings reveals how the same activity takes different forms, from vegetable beds to indoor collections.
concepts.original_description: Growing and caring for plants in gardens and small outdoor spaces.

concepts.label: Composting
concepts.learning_takeaway: Connect a compost pile’s ingredients and heat to microbial decomposition.
concepts.card: Composting manages the breakdown of food scraps and plant material into a soil amendment. Microorganisms need carbon, nitrogen, moisture, and oxygen. A pile’s rising temperature offers a concrete way to explore the biological activity that turns discarded material into compost.
concepts.original_description: Turning organic waste into nutrient-rich material for soil.

evidence.locator: What is Composting?; Ingredients; Steps for Backyard Composting, step 5

concepts.label: Seed saving
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand why pollination and parentage affect what saved seeds grow into.
concepts.card: Seed saving keeps seeds for later planting. Many vegetable seeds are dried for storage. Pollination history matters: hybrid offspring may differ from their parents, while an open-pollinated variety can stay similar when pollinated within that variety. The next generation makes heredity visible.
concepts.original_description: Collecting and preserving plant seeds for future growing seasons.

evidence.locator: Quick facts; Open-pollinated plants; Hybrid plants; Storing your saved seeds

concepts.label: Agroforestry
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize several ways trees are intentionally integrated into agricultural production.
concepts.card: Agroforestry deliberately combines trees or shrubs with crops or livestock. Its different arrangements include alley cropping, forest farming, and silvopasture. Comparing these practices offers a way to explore how agriculture and forestry can occupy the same managed landscape.
concepts.original_description: Growing trees alongside crops or livestock in integrated agricultural systems.

evidence.locator: Background Information and History, final paragraph

concepts.label: Fermentation (food processing)
concepts.learning_takeaway: Compare the distinct food transformations created by microbial products.
concepts.card: Food fermentation uses desired microbial activity to transform ingredients. Different products reveal different effects: carbon dioxide helps bread rise, while organic acids contribute flavor and preservation in foods such as sauerkraut. The same broad practice can change taste, texture, or keeping qualities.
concepts.original_description: Using microorganisms to transform and preserve foods.

evidence.note: Supports intentional microbial activity, bread leavening, acids and sauerkraut, flavor, texture, and preservation.

concepts.label: Sourdough
concepts.learning_takeaway: Link sourdough’s tang and leavening with its microbial partners.
concepts.card: Sourdough uses a fermenting mixture in which wild yeasts and lactic acid bacteria act on flour’s carbohydrates. Their activity produces the dough’s tang and gas that helps it rise. Exploring these partners connects a loaf’s flavor and expansion to a microbial community.
concepts.original_description: Baking with naturally maintained cultures of yeast and bacteria.

evidence.note: Supports wild yeast, lactic acid bacteria, carbohydrate breakdown, tang, carbon dioxide and dough rise.

relations.note: The inspected extension passage explicitly describes sourdough as fermentation.

imported_records.description: Baking with naturally maintained cultures of yeast and bacteria.

concepts.label: Pickling
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish fermentation-produced acidity from directly added vinegar in pickling.
concepts.card: Pickling includes more than one route to acidic food. Fermented pickles develop acidity as they cure; quick-process pickles receive vinegar without fermentation. Comparing the two reveals why similar sour flavors can arise through different processes, and why acidity also matters to food safety.
concepts.original_description: Preserving foods in acidic solutions or through fermentation.

evidence.note: Supports the two methods and the significance of acidity for taste and safety.

concepts.learning_takeaway: Trace the interaction between leavening gas and dough structure during baking.
concepts.card: Bread baking turns dough into a solid loaf through heat. In yeast-raised wheat bread, fermentation supplies gas and gluten helps trap it. Following the dough into the oven reveals how expanding gas and a setting structure produce the loaf’s familiar texture.

concepts.card: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian monk who investigated inheritance by crossing pea plants and tracking their descendants. Exploring his experiments shows how counted offspring can expose regularities that casual family resemblance does not explain.

concepts.label: Cognitive psychology
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize concept formation and problem solving as examples of cognitive research.
concepts.card: Cognitive psychology investigates mental processes such as thinking, perception, memory, and language. Questions about how people form concepts or choose a way to solve a problem make the field concrete, connecting everyday acts of understanding with the study of how the mind works.
concepts.original_description: Studying mental processes such as attention, memory and reasoning.

concepts.label: Confirmation bias
concepts.learning_takeaway: Recognize unequal attention to belief-supporting and belief-challenging evidence.
concepts.card: Confirmation bias is a tendency to favor information that fits existing beliefs. A person who already dislikes a teacher may notice rude moments while overlooking friendly interactions. Exploring this imbalance shows how selective attention to evidence can reinforce an established impression.
concepts.original_description: Examining the tendency to favor information that supports existing beliefs.

evidence.note: Definition and professor example support all descriptive claims; the takeaway reframes the same selection imbalance.

concepts.label: Curiosity
concepts.learning_takeaway: Investigate how partial knowledge relates to curiosity in a specific experimental task.
concepts.card: Curiosity concerns the motivation to seek information. In a trivia experiment discussed by Kidd and Hayden, people were most curious when moderately confident about an answer. Exploring this pattern raises a question: how does partial knowledge shape the desire to learn more?
concepts.original_description: Studying the motivation to seek information, novelty and understanding.

evidence.locator: Abstract; Figure 1 caption summarizing Kang et al. (2009)
evidence.note: Abstract supports information-seeking motivation; Figure 1 explicitly reports the moderate-confidence trivia finding. The result is scoped to that experiment.

concepts.label: Habit formation
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish gradual automaticity and individual variation from fixed-day habit claims.
concepts.card: Habit formation concerns the growth of automatic responses through repetition in a consistent context. In one daily-behavior study, modeled automaticity rose toward a plateau at different rates across participants. Exploring those differences shows why repeated behavior does not follow a universal formation timetable.
concepts.original_description: Understanding how repeated behaviors become automatic over time.

evidence.note: Abstract supports consistent-context repetition, modeled asymptotic automaticity and variable times. Wording identifies one study and avoids advice or a universal duration.

relations.note: Editorial navigation: Automaticity and repeated behavior offer a cognitive-psychology connection.

imported_records.description: Understanding how repeated behaviors become automatic over time.

concepts.label: Stroop effect
concepts.learning_takeaway: Understand the task comparison used to measure word–color interference.
concepts.card: The Stroop effect appears when conflicting word meanings interfere with naming ink colors. For example, saying the ink color of “red” printed in blue requires ignoring the word. Comparing color-naming times with and without those conflicting words makes interference between responses measurable.
concepts.original_description: effect of psychological interference on reaction time

evidence.locator: Problem statement; Experiment 2, materials and results, original pages 650–652
evidence.note: Stroop’s problem statement gives the red/blue example; Experiment 2 compares conflicting words with color squares and reports slower naming.

relations.note: Editorial navigation: The interference task provides an experimental example of cognitive processes.

concepts.label: Conjunction fallacy
concepts.learning_takeaway: Distinguish a convincing description from the probability of an event contained within another.
concepts.card: The conjunction fallacy occurs when a combined event is judged more probable than one of its components. The classic Linda problem compares “bank teller” with “bank teller and feminist.” Exploring why the richer description can seem more plausible separates representativeness from the mathematical rule governing probability.
concepts.original_description: formal fallacy that occurs when it is assumed that specific conditions are more probable than a single general one

evidence.locator: Abstract, original p. 293; Linda problem and direct comparisons, pp. 297–299 (PDF pp. 5–7)
evidence.note: Abstract states the rule and representativeness account; Linda comparisons document the judgment pattern.

relations.note: Editorial navigation: The fallacy contrasts intuitive judgment with probability’s conjunction rule.
